order, I wish to draw your attention to a statement, as reported in Hansard, made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) last night. I had referred to a speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs made on May 2 in Renfrew, as to which the press report carried the statement that he had referred to "hoop-la diplomacy" and vaudeville performances; and I had indicated my belief that these words did not properly describe the type of diplomacy that was being discussed. Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as reported at page 3007 of Hansard, said this:
If the leader of the opposition had read my speech and not a newspaper account of the speech into the records of Hansard he might have'come to a different conclusion concerning it.
In view of. that statement, I sent to his office this morning for a text of the speech and was informed that there was no text. The newspaper report was therefore the only record available. But in reading the text of Hansard I also noticed that the Secretary of State for External Affairs had said that he made a similar speech in Toronto on April 10; and I obtained the text of that speech. In his remarks last night-

speechtext:
I have no intention of reopening the debate, Mr. Speaker. I am simply correcting the record. The Secretary of State for External Affairs last night, in reference to my statement that the term "hoop-la diplomacy" had been used, said:
I quoted from a paragraph by the columnist, Mr. Walter Lippmann, written some weeks before these events.
He then quoted that columnist. On reading the text of the similar speech to which he referred as having been substantially the same as the one in Renfrew, I find that while later in the speech he quoted from Mr. Lippmann, these are his own words:
In the circumstances of the present, it will, I think, have a better chance of reaching these goals if we abandon what has been called "hoop-la diplomacy," at Lake Success, at Ottawa, or, I hasten to add, at Tokyo.
He then went on to use further words, and in the latter part of the paragraph he said:
That is only one reason why I hope that in this country we will resolutely refuse to countenance the methods or the atmosphere of the circus or the vaudeville theatre in our conduct of popular and democratic government. Dignity is an important element of democracy.
I have read these quotations, Mr. Speaker, as a matter of privilege in order to correct the record; and may I suggest that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would be well advised to be more accurate in the comments in his speeches.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution: That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the administration of Laurier house, in the city of Ottawa, and of an account to be set up in the consolidated revenue fund to be known as the Mackenzie King trust account to which shall be credited the sum of $225,000 given by the will of the late the Right Honourable William Lyon Mackenzie King, P.C., O.M., to the government of Canada, to be expended for the purposes of such administration.
Laurier House
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members, will recall the circumstances which are responsible for the legislation the government is proposing in this resolution, and in the accompanying resolution concerning the Kingsmere property which I propose to bring forward as soon as this one has been disposed of. I am sure, however, that all hon. members would wish to have the sequence of events set out in the permanent records of parliament. It is as follows:
On August 7 last I was given a copy of the last will and testament of my predecessor the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. On August 8, when Mr. King's will was made public, I gave a statement to the press which I should like to read. It is as follows:
I was advised yesterday by his executors of the disposition which Mr. Mackenzie King had made in his will of those properties which with forethought and generosity he determined many years before his death should become a trust for the people of Canada.
I at once recommended to my colleagues in the government that we should formally express our grateful acknowledgment of these bequests, and a minute of council has duly recorded our appreciation and our readiness to accept in the name of the Canadian people the necessary transfers and trust deeds. I am confident that all future governments will be as pleased as we are to see that Mr. King's wishes respecting the use of these public trusts are completely fulfilled.
The statement went on:
Their creation is a further evidence of Mr. King's high ideals of service to his country. The people of Canada will always be grateful for the endowment of the national capital by the perpetuation of the historic treasure which Laurier house has already come to be, by the generous provision towards the cost of its care and maintenance, and by the magnificent addition of the Kingsmere properties to the national domain.
The dedication by Mr. King of the residue of his estate for post-graduate scholarships will also commend itself to all who knew him, as a most fitting way to commemorate his deep interest in education, and the scholarly tradition which was so dear to him. Mr. King's will is a most notable example of the careful stewardship, the sense of history and the love of country, which distinguished his life and now enriches our Canadian heritage.
I should like also to read the text of the minute of council referred' to in the statement. It is as follows:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report dated August 7, 1950, from the Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent, the Prime Minister, submitting that he has been advised by the executors that the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, in his last will and testament, bequeathed the property in the city of Ottawa known as Laurier house, together with a capital sum to assist in its upkeep, and his properties at Kingsmere, to become public trusts for the benefit of the people of Canada.
The Prime Minister recommends that the executors be advised of the grateful acknowledgment of these bequests by the government on behalf of the

Laurier House
people of Canada, and that the appropriate authorities be duly authorized to accept the necessary transfers and trust deeds from the executors.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
Some weeks later the executors initiated discussions with the government to arrange for the formal transfer of property, and we began at the same time to give consideration to the most appropriate means of administering the bequest of Laurier house and the property at Kingsmere. In view of the quite different purposes of the two bequests, the government felt it would be preferable to introduce separate measures covering each. The resolution under consideration relates to the administration of Laurier house.
It might be helpful in consideration of the resolution and of the bill founded upon it if I were to read the portions of Mr. King's will relating to Laurier house. They read as follows:
13.	For many years it has been my intention to bequeath Laurier house to the government and people of Canada, in the belief that as the years pass, the citizens of Canada will take an increasing interest and pride in the preservation of a house occupied through many years by two of Canada's prime ministers and reminiscent of an environment that was a part of their daily lives.
14.	It has been my hope that such a bequest might serve also to remind my fellow Canadians of the close association I enjoyed with Sir Wilfrid and Lady Laurier, and what I owed to their personal friendship; also to emphasize the unity of heart and mind among the Canadian people which Sir Wilfrid and I throughout our years of office, sought to preserve in the administration of Canada's national affairs.
15.	The maintenance of the residence as a place of historic interest and contemporary record of days that are gone would also serve the interests of the Canadian people in other ways. The residence might appropriately, I think, be given an immediate association with the Public Archives of Canada. Responsibility for its continued preservation, supervision and use might be placed upon the dominion archivist. Accommodation for scholars engaged on work of research in Ottawa is at present most inadequate both at the archives and at the library of parliament. In the years of my occupancy of Laurier house, I have done most of my work in the library and adjoining rooms on the top floor. I should particularly welcome the continued use of this portion of the house for purposes of study and research. A direct association with the archives would not only serve to emphasize the historic significance of the residence, but would help to ensure the interior being maintained such as it is, and would lead naturally to a more appropriate display of important documents and other objects of special interest. I should hope that the dining room and its furnishings, paintings, etc., would be retained much as they are.
16.	I therefore give, devise and bequeath to the government of Canada in trust for the people of Canada the house situated at 335 Laurier avenue east in the city of Ottawa, and all the contents of the said house except such papers, books, furnishings and other things for the disposal of which I have made provision otherwise in this my will.
17.	I also give, devise and bequeath to the government of Canada in trust for the people of Canada the sum of two hundred and twenty-five thousand

dollars ($225,000), the interest thereon to be used to assist in the maintenance and care of the said house. The said sum of two hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars ($225,000) represents moneys which the Hon. Peter C. Larkin and other friends contributed, after the reconstruction and refurnishing of the residence was completed, to assist me in its upkeep throughout my life, and in meeting, to the end of my life, other personal and public needs, especially such needs as would arise in years of retirement.
I think it will be apparent that, as the resolution, itself puts it, it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the administration of Laurier house and of the trust fund bequeathed by Mr. King to assist in the maintenance and care of Laurier house.
I feel it would be preferable for me to reserve any further observations until the house has disposed of the resolution and there is available for the consideration of hon. members the bill setting out the provisions which we think would be appropriate to carry out the intentions of the will. I should then be quite happy to try to explain any of the provisions which might not be felt to be self-evident.
I should like to conclude by expressing the conviction that hon. members in all parts of the house will wish to associate themselves with the government in making appropriate provisions for the administration of this permanent memorial of two of our country's former prime ministers.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Dion in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should
like to make one or two comments. First of all, may I say that I think iall hon. members feel it is appropriate to take this action at the present time. I am sure there will be approval of the provision made by the Minister of Public Works, when the bill is passed, to see to it that this house, which has historic interest for the people of Canada, will be properly maintained and that any necessary improvements in the house and the area it occupies will be made. I pass Laurier house every day, and two or three weeks ago I was pleased to see a group of men working to improve the grounds. The new hedge, the tulips, the flowers and so on will make the house and grounds much more attractive. But the Minister of Public Works should see that the exterior of the house is gone over, because as it is now it does not look like a very appropriate memorial. A good deal of repair and renovation is needed on the outside.
I merely intended to say that we wish to associate ourselves with the remarks of the Prime Minister in regard to this matter, and

to express the hope that Laurier house will be used as a place of study and research by those who are interested in a most important period in Canada's history which coincided with the prime ministership, not only of Mr. Mackenzie King but of his great predecessor, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I am sure that hon. members are most happy to see progress made with this measure and steps being taken to create this memorial of the late prime minister.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OP BEQUEST TO GOVERNMENT OF CANADA UNDER THE WILL OF THE LATE MR. MACKENZIE KING
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the administration of Kingsmere park by the federal district commission and the management and control of the buildings in the park and the yards, orchards and appurtenances thereto by the Minister of Public Works in accordance with the will of the late the Right Honourable William Lyon Mackenzie King, P.C., O.M., with authority in the governor in council to set aside any part of the park as a country home for the holder of the office of prime minister, such park to be deemed included in the properties described in the schedule to the Prime Minister's Residence Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this resolution I feel there is little I can add to what I have said already on the previous resolution respecting Laurier house, but I think it would be helpful in this case, as in the other, to place on record the relevant portions of Mr. Mackenzie King's will concerning Kingsmere park. They are as follows:
24.	The cherished objective of being able to
present my Kingsmere properties as a thank offering for what has come to me in the way of opportunities of public service, I believe I have been able to realize, and I hereby bequeath to the government of Canada as a public park in trust for the citizens of Canada, subject to certain reservations hereinafter referred to, my several properties at Kingsmere, in the province of Quebec, amounting in all to nearly five hundred acres, and the houses and other buildings erected thereon. The precise boundaries are set forth in the several deeds attached hereto.	'
25.	In making this bequest, I express the wish that the lands at Kingsmere may be maintained as nearly as possible in their present state: that they will be developed as parkland, and that they will form a wild life sanctuary and will continue to have the character of a natural forest reserve.
26.	Believing that my successors in the office of prime minister may find, as I have found, a renewal of strength in this quiet place, as well as exceptional opportunities for conference on national and international affairs, I hope that the government of Canada will consider the possibility of setting aside a part of the Kingsmere property as a country home for the holder of the office of Prime Minister of Canada.
27.	Inasmuch as relatives and friends of mine have spent their summers, or part of them, at Kingsmere as my guests or tenants. I hope they may continue to enjoy the summer homes to which they have become accustomed; and that other appropriate use may be made of them. I would therefore ask that the government should authorize my trustees to provide that, for a period of three years after my death, the cottages and such of their contents as are mine and are not otherwise disposed of in accordance with this my will shall be available, rent free, for use by my sister and the members of her family, by the members of my late brother's family, and by such other persons as may be designated by my trustees.
28.	My trustees are hereby authorized to dispose of all my possessions in the cottages and other

Kingsmere Park
buildings or on the property as they believe will be most in accord with my own wishes; and to meet such expenses as may be necessarily incurred for the maintenance of these cottages for a period of three years.
X am sure hon. members will agree that the federal district commission, which has the responsibility of the development of the national capital and of the Gatineau park, is the appropriate body to be entrusted with the administration of the properties which will constitute Kingsmere park and ultimately form an integral part of a parkway system, the whole of which will help to preserve the memory of Mr. Mackenzie King and of his interest in the creation of this parkway system around the national capital.
I do not feel there is anything I need add in moving the resolution, as it will obviously be more convenient for hon. members to discuss what is proposed when they have the text of the bill before them.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Dion in the chair.

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OP BEQUEST TO GOVERNMENT OF CANADA UNDER THE WILL OF THE LATE MR. MACKENZIE KING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I said something about Laurier house, and I am sure it is with much pleasure that we see that property set aside for the purposes indicated. Nevertheless I think this is a more important bequest to the country in many respects than Laurier house. It has not the same historic significance, but it is a valuable addition to the national capital project. I think those of us who are familiar with the beauty of the area on the Quebec side of the Ottawa river thus bequeathed to this country will appreciate to the fullest extent what this will mean in the days to come to the people of Ottawa and the people of Canada. The people of Canada should be fully informed of the value of this bequest, one of our beauty spots, to the nation. I suppose that one day, which probably none of us here will see, Canada will possess the most beautifully situated and developed capital in the whole world. There is no lovelier site, and this bequest is certainly an important addition to the federal district. I hope that the people of Canada will appreciate what it means.
May I also say that the provision in the will requesting the setting aside of a piece of this property for a country home for present and future prime ministers is a suggestion that is well worth while. Before the resolution passes through the committee stage, may I say again that this is probably one of the most important bequests that has been made to our country. I am quite sure that in the days to come many thousands of Canadians, indeed through the years many

millions, will learn to love the beautiful area which includes the Kingsmere property in the delightful Gatineau district.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. St. Laurent thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 290, respecting Kingsmere park.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO COMPENSATION BOARDS, ADMINISTRATION CHANGES, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO COMPENSATION BOARDS, ADMINISTRATION CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Government Employees Compensation Act, 1947, to provide authority to make accountable advances to provincial workmen's compensation boards on account of expenses incurred by such boards in the investigation and adjudication of claims undertaken by arrangement with the federal government; and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, this resolution
announces the intention to make a few amendments to the Government Employees Compensation Act, 1947. That act made provision for the payment of compensation to employees of the crown in right of Canada where the employee is caused personal injury by accident arising out of and in the course of his employment, or is disabled by reason of an industrial disease due to the nature of his employment. In case of death of the employee resulting from such an accident or industrial disease, his dependents are entitled to compensation under the act. The provisions of the act also apply to employees of corporations, commissions, boards or agencies established to perform a function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada, who are brought within the scope of the act by order of the governor in council.
The general principle of the act is that the compensation benefits payable thereunder shall be the same as is provided in the case of employees employed in private industry, or dependents of a deceased employee under the law of the province in which the accident occurs or the industrial disease is contracted. The application of the present act to employees in the Northwest Territories required the enactment of special provisions therein, in view no doubt of the lack at that time of adequate local workmen's compensation legislation in the general area.

The present act provides in effect that compensation shall be payable to employees of the crown ordinarily resident in the Yukon Territory or the Northwest Territories, and to dependents of deceased employees who were so resident, in accordance with the compensation legislation in force in the Yukon Territory. This has had the effect of providing uniform treatment and benefits for employees of the crown resident in these unorganized areas. However, it has been strongly represented by departments of government who have resident employees in the Northwest Territories that these provisions of the act do not provide adequate benefits for employees in the area under present-day conditions, and provide less favourable treatment for employees in both the Northwest Territories and the Yukon than is provided under the act for employees of the crown elsewhere in Canada.
The provinces are able to provide and administer more comprehensive compensation benefits under their workmen's compensation legislation on a self-sustaining basis than it has been found feasible to provide in the Yukon and Northwest Territories under the workmen's compensation legislation in force in these areas. Consequently the discrepancy between the benefits payable under the act to employees of the crown ordinarily resident in the territories and the benefits payable to employees of the crown under the act elsewhere in Canada is serious and substantial.
Following a review of the situation, in the light of the representations which have been made the government has considered it advisable to introduce amendments to the act which will bring the provisions for compensation benefits for employees resident in the Yukon and Northwest Territories in line with benefits payable under the act to employees of the crown resident elsewhere in Canada. The major amendments here proposed give effect to the foregoing by providing that hereafter employees of the crown ordinarily resident in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon Territory, and dependents of deceased employees who were so resident, shall be entitled to compensation under the act in accordance with the provisions of the laws of the province of Alberta applicable to employees in private industry.
The provisions of the Alberta legislation have been designated as applicable for the purposes of the act because of the proximity of this province to the territories, and the fact that to an increasing extent the greater part of the movement of personnel and the normal lines of travel and communication in and out of the greater part of these territories are by way of Alberta. Moreover, in the
Government Employees Compensation Act administration of the act for the benefit of employees in the territories it is felt that claims arising in the territories can be dealt with and adjudicated with a minimum of delay by the application of the Alberta compensation provisions. The provisions for compensation under the Alberta legislation are considered to be appropriate for application to employees in the territories. The provisions will continue to ensure uniformity of treatment for employees resident in either the Yukon or Northwest Territories.
It may be recalled that up until 1950 the claims of employees of the crown employed in Prince Edward Island were dealt with under the provisions of the neighbouring province of New Brunswick, because of the absence, prior to that time, of comprehensive provincial workmen's compensation legislation in Prince Edward Island. This is a similar administrative provision which is intended to be adopted in this case.
The other proposed amendments to the act are of a minor and technical nature.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADVANCES TO COMPENSATION BOARDS, ADMINISTRATION CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of this resolution, which precedes legislation amending the Government Employees Compensation Act, 1947.
First may I commend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) for bringing in this legislation, which no doubt will correct an iniquitous situation affecting government employees in the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory. At the present time if an employee of the federal government meets with an accident while in the performance of his duty in any province, he is generally entitled to such compensations as would be paid under the terms of the Workmen's Compensation Act of the province in which the accident occurred, or the province in which he normally resides. However, where an employee ordinarily resident in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory meets with an accident, he receives such compensation as is provided for by the workmen's compensation ordinance of the Yukon Territory.
Whatever the reason or excuse, there is no doubt that the provisions of the workmen's compensation ordinance of the Yukon Territory are much less generous than similar legislation in the provinces adjacent to the
3034	HOUSE OF
Government Employees Compensation Act Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory. Under the terms of the ordinance there is no provision for the payment of any pension whatever to the dependents of a workman who is fatally injured, or to a workman who may be permanently injured; and that is a sad state of affairs. The ordinance does provide that in the event of the death of a workman resulting from injury, his dependents shall be entitled to receive the sum of $5,000, with $750 to each dependent child of the deceased under the age of sixteen, the total not to exceed the sum of $8,600. When a workman receives an injury arising out of and in the course of his employment as a result of which he is totally and permanently disabled, he shall be entitled to receive as compensation the sum of $6,000. Certain stated lesser amounts are payable in the case of other injuries. For instance, the loss of a hand or foot is valued at $3,000, while an arm or leg is valued at $4,000. There is no workmen's compensation board to administer this ordinance, and to which the injured workman or his dependents may apply for compensation. Every employer is required to enter into and maintain a contract of insurance providing for the payment of compensation to his employees and their dependents, and they must take proceedings for recovery. The ordinance makes no provision for the medical or surgical care of the injured workman, nor does it apply where less than five workmen are employed in the same general employment.
It is grossly unfair that federal employees and others whose duties take them to the more northern (parts of Canada, where by the very nature of things, owing to the remoteness and lack of transportation facilities, the hazards of employment are greater than in the more settled parts of our country, should be further penalized by having to come under the provisions of such deplorable legislation as the Yukon workmen's compensation ordinance if they are so unfortunate as to meet with an accident. Let us take an actual case.
Dr. Michael Feniak was resident geologist at Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories for the geological survey of Canada, a man of high professional qualifications, active in community life, and altogether an admirable Canadian of whom we might all be proud. In July, 1949, he was drowned while employed on hazardous governmental work. He was a young man, with a wife and two small children, one of whom was born only a few days prior to his fatal accident. He had not been long enough in the government service to build up much credit under the superannuation act. All his widow and children were entitled to was $5,000 for the widow and


$750 for each of the children, or a total of $6,500, under the terms of the workmen's compensation ordinance of the Yukon Territory. This was the pittance this family received as compensation for the loss of a husband and father. However, I am pleased to say that the federal government gave a special gratuity of $2,000 on compassionate grounds in 1950, authorized by this parliament. This very fact is an admission that the present legislation covering compensation for government employees in northern Canada is inadequate, and I welcome this amending legislation as a means of alleviating this deplorable condition.
During the course of my remarks I have mentioned some of the inadequacies of the present legislation covering workmen's compensation in the Yukon Territory. I am told it is not much better in the Northwest Territories, and I would bring the situation to the attention of the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), who is responsible for the administration of the northern territories. I am aware of the difficulties presented by the sparse population and the relatively small number of employers and employees as compared with some of the provinces. These same difficulties make it expensive for insurance companies to operate in the territories; therefore the rates for adequate coverage are high. These difficulties should be and can be surmounted.
I am pleased to learn that the Department of Resources and Development has a committee of officers studying the problems of workmen's compensation in the Northwest Territories. The committee has held several meetings already, and has obtained information from provincial compensation authorities and from insurance companies writing compensation business. It has also ascertained the opinions of employers of labour in the provinces and the territories in the mining, lumbering, fishing and transportation industries.
Though the terms of the workmen's compensation ordinance of the Northwest Territories are much more favourable than those of the Yukon Territory, the present system is inadequate. The Northwest Territories ordinance provides for compensation by insurance, with a limit of $15,000 for any person and $105,000 for any accident. These limits in the past have proved insufficient, and I believe the problem under consideration is how to render the system adequate. This resolution provides only for compensation for government employees killed or injured in the course of duty in the Northwest Territories or Yukon; it does not provide compensation for non-government workmen in those territories on a scale comparable to

that provided in. the other provinces of Canada. With the exception of the province of Prince Edward Island, all the other original provinces have a reasonably comparable system of compensation for workmen killed or injured in the course of their employment.
A general summary shows that on an average, based on a maximum salary of $2,500 per annum, for compensation purposes, workmen during their period of incapacity receive 66f per cent of their average earning up to the maximum allowable of $2,500. Funeral expenses varying from $125 to $175 are allowed. Widows receive from $40 to $50 per month, with from $10 to $15 per month for each child, depending upon the province.
If the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory are to expand, as we all expect they will, the fact that adequate workmen's compensation is not available will definitely tend to discourage capable workmen, who are conscious of their obligations to their wives and families, from seeking employment in those territories; and these are of the type the territories should encourage to settle there.
I believe the solution is to establish in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory a full-scale workmen's compensation scheme in accordance with the provision contained in workmen's compensation acts in the other provinces of Canada, preferably British Columbia. I prefer British Columbia for the reason that the mining industry of the north is largely an extension of that in British Columbia. Therefore legislation providing compensation for employees engaged in placer mining, deep lode mining or smelter or mill occupations should be the same in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory as in British Columbia. I refer particularly to silicosis and lead poisoning as occupational diseases which are provided for under the British Columbia Workmen's Compensation Act. I see no reason why the good people of our north country should not be entitled to receive the same benefits as those received by people residing in the several provinces. The legislation now in force in the territories is nothing more than rank discrimination and surely should not be tolerated any longer.
I am strongly of the opinion that, owing to the similarity of the conditions and types of industry in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, a workmen's compensation scheme should apply with equal benefits in both areas.
The north, which is the last reservoir of mineral resources in North America-it has
15, 1351	3035
Government Employees Compensation Act hardly been scratched, or even thoroughly prospected-is now coming into its own with the opening of new mines and the expansion of older ones. All this will lead to an increase in population which will make it easier to put into operation more generous legislation affecting workmen's compensation, with the ultimate object of having properly organized workmen's compensation boards in operation. This will have to be done if we are going to get people to go into the north to develop its resources; and now is the time to start doing something about it.
I am therefore glad to support this resolution, which is an honest endeavour to correct this injustice in so far as it relates to government employees; and I hope that similar legislation will be enacted at an early day to provide proper benefits for non-government workmen on a scale comparable to those provided in the provinces of Canada, preferably British Columbia.

I wish to make a brief statement in relation to the bill because I believe this is the time to draw attention again to our policy in an effort to find a real solution for this whole question. I can only repeat what I have said before. As I indicated earlier in the session, and in previous sessions as well, I have a strong conviction that there is great inconsistency in asserting our belief that full equality should be established for the peoples of other lands, asserting that as though we thought that principle could be carried into practice in other lands, when in this democracy of ours we have failed to solve this one problem which has to do with the measure of equality that is to be extended to a very large number of our own citizens.
I would point out that the number affected by this bill is not insignificant. It happens that the number is almost the same as the total population of Iceland, an independent nation with a long and proud history. I employ that comparison only by way of illustration to point out that we are dealing with a large number of human beings who have all the qualifications to become equal citizens in every respect of this country of ours.
I realize that some opinions are held among the Indian tribes that they do not wish the treaty relationships to be unduly disturbed. They regard these as sacred contractual rights which they wish preserved, along with all the privileges and protections of certain kinds which they receive under the treaty contracts. On the other hand, whatever views may be expressed, either by members of the Indian tribes affected or by other Canadians, we cannot be satisfied until we have established a basis of absolute equality for all Canadians in this country.
Once again I simply want to place on record, while the bill is under consideration, the opinion that no hon. member should have in his mind the thought that we have done more than improve an unsatisfactory situation. Undoubtedly the amendments that have been placed before the house, and that have been improved by reference to the committee

which has spent some time on the bill, will be to the advantage of the Indian population of Canada affected by this measure.
I wish to express my own belief that the minister has approached this subject with a real desire to improve the lot of the Indian members of the Canadian population. While we adopt the bill, to whatever extent it is adopted, as a measure that will improve the position of those affected by it, I wish to leave the thought that all of us should be directing our attention to the way in which we can bring the Indian population fully into the regular citizenship of Canada, protecting them in so far as their basic rights are concerned but at the same time giving them the opportunities of education and of ordinary citizenship which I am convinced they are capable of accepting and of carrying forward with success in the years ahead.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it would be useful if the minister would summarize the amendments which were made in committee so that the public, and particularly the Indians, may know what changes have been made since the bill was first introduced.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe it is appropriate on section 1 to make any general comments about the bill. speechtext:
Without desiring to interrupt my hon. friend, may I indicate to him that we have not yet dealt with the estimates of the Indian affairs branch. While I know that what he is going to say will be

with Bill No. 79. Bill 79 had not been formulated; it had not been introduced. No legislation amending the Indian Act was before that committee, so that all the committee had an opportunity to do was to give general consideration to the question of Indian affairs and to ways in which the former Indian Act might be amended.
Then we had Bill No. 267 introduced last year. I believe it is perfectly accurate to say that Bill No. 267 was not found to be acceptable. You will remember, Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee will recall, that the bill was not proceeded with after its introduction late in the spring of 1950. Now we have Bill 79 which again in fairness must be said to be an improvement in certain respects over Bill 267. The minister did call nineteen representative Indians, I think it was, to a conference. That conference, however, was held with the minister and officials of his department. No members of the house were in attendance, and there was no opportunity for the Indians themselves as a body to appear before the house or a committee of the house to present their views.
Therefore when the present Bill 79 was before the special committee set up this session there had been no representations by Indians to that committee as to their attitude with respect to the bill and how it might be further improved. It is an unfortunate fact that there are a large number of responsible Indians who feel that Bill 79 does not go as far as it might to improve the general position of Indians in this country. The bill, however, was fully considered by the committee, and I do not propose at this time to repeat all the arguments Which were advanced in the committee, because after all it is the purpose of such a committee that these arguments shall take place so that the bill may receive detailed consideration. Generally speaking, although not in any sense depriving members of the house of the right to full expression in the house, certainly it is at least logical to expect that the house will accept the work of such a special committee.
That being the case, I think it is doubly to be regretted that Indian representatives did not have an opportunity to appear before the committee. I might say at this point that twice during its proceedings motions were made that Indian witnesses be called, once at the first sitting of the committee before we embarked upon the detailed consideration of the bill, and the second time When the committee had considered the bill clause by clause and was about to bring its proceedings to a close. On each occasion it was formally moved that the committee, in addition to any other witnesses who might 80709-194J
Indian Act
be heard, should call upon Indian representatives to oome and give us the benefit of their views with respect to this legislation. On each occasion these motions were defeated by a majority of the members of the committee.
I think it is a pity that the bill, which is so important to the Indians, should be passed, first through the committee and now through the house without that opportunity having: been given. The history of the Indian Act, as I recall art, shows that the act has only-received major amendment on an average of about once every twenty years since it was first enacted. That is a very rough average, but I think it will be found to be the approximate interval between major amendments of thi3 legislation. Therefore this is long-term legislation.
This is legislation under which a very substantial number of men, women and children living in Canada will be governed. Therefore, now that the problem of Indian affairs has been brought before this house in a way it has not been for twenty years, at any rate now that our attitude toward Indian affairs has made a considerable advance, as I believe it has, and now that we are coming to believe, to insist and have it generally accepted that Indians can and should be made equal, it seems to me doubly important that the very people who are going to live under this legislation should have had the opportunity to appear before the committee and express their views as to the details of the legislation under which, if past history is anything of a guide, they will have to live for perhaps the next twenty years.
It is true that the committee did pass a resolution, in the form of an amendment to one of the motions to which I have referred, in which they said that the Indian Act should be reviewed at the end of two years. When the motion was made that we hear Indian representatives an amendment was moved that we should not hear the representatives at this time, but that the committee was of the opinion that the Indian Act should be reviewed at the end of two years. That, however, was only an expression of opinion by the committee, and I think I am correct in saying it does not have the force of law. It rests with the government and minister to decide whether or not the act will be subject to a general review at that time. So there is no assurance in that amendment that Indians will have an opportunity as a body, through their organizations, to have a thorough review of this legislation at the end of two years. As I say, past history shows that this legislation is not

Indian Act
thoroughly reviewed and subject to major amendments on an average of more than once every twenty years.
I express this opinion because, while I do not wish to dissent from the work done by the committee in so far as it improved the legislation, I do wish any acceptance of this legislation on my part at the present time to be subject to the reservation that it probably could have been further improved if the Indian representatives had been brought here and heard, and also to the further reservation that in that case no Indian or anyone else could suggest that the Indians were not fully and properly consulted and their views and wishes ascertained with respect to this legislation.
I should like to ask the minister what assurances can be given or whether in fact he will give an assurance that so long as he is minister he intends to accept that recommendation of the Indian affairs committee that the act be subject to review at the end of two years and that a parliamentary committee be set up at that time to hear from the minister and his officials on the operation of the new act we are putting through the aouse today.

speechtext: After listening to the remarks of the last speaker I do not know Whether those who sat on the committee for the last three or four years share the opinion I hold. I believe representatives of all Indian tribes throughout Canada were given .[DOT]every opportunity to place their problems before the committee; and I think the committee did marvellous work. Now the hon. member seems to wish to leave the impression with the house that all Indians were not given full opportunity to bring their problems to that committee. I d:o not believe the last speaker was a member of the old committee, and. I do not think he can have read all the evidence that was adduced before that committee. The members of that committee sat patiently during many sessions; and if this year it was not thought desirable to re-examine all the subjects we had already covered so thoroughly it was because we did not want to delay the legislation, which we thought implemented all the conclusions at which the committee had arrived. So I do not think the impression should be left with this house that the Indians did not have full opportunity to make their representations. I dare say the legislation is not perfect, but as with any other legislation it can be corrected in future if any correction is necessary.

hon. member for Kamloops. We discussed the matter of the further revision of the act, and on more than one occasion I gave the assurance that we would not have a long period between revisions. When we discussed the question of again interviewing the Indians I gave a categorical answer to a question put me by one of the other members of the committee. That appears at page 280 of the committee's proceedings. It seems to me the wording of the resolution goes a little further than that, in that the committee recommended that the Indian Act be reviewed in two years' time. I am quite sure that every member of the committee would agree that the officials of the Indian affairs branch, through the very fact of exercising their functions, must have the act before them every day, and to that extent it is being reviewed constantly. In the light of that fact the recommendation of a special committee of the house considering whether or not we should hear further evidence now, which expressed the conclusion that we should not hear further evidence now but that the Indian Act should be reviewed at the end of two years, I think must be taken to mean much more than a mere departmental review. I think it must mean the opportunity by a committee of this house to review the act at the end of two years. Certainly that is the sense in which

I took that resolution. I wonder if I am right in taking from the minister's latest answer that he understands the motion merely to mean that the act should be reviewed by the department, possibly with Indian representatives called in from time to time, or whether he does not think it means that the members of this house should have an opportunity in two years' time to make a further detailed study of the Indian Act.

This committee is of the opinion that no further evidence is now required for our purposes, but that we recommend that further consideration be given to the Indian Act in two years' time.
Having stated earlier that the government would reconvene a conference of Indians, I assumed that was what the committee had in mind. I did not take this to be a direction, that a special committee should be appointed; but if that is what hon. members had in mind I am quite sure they will bring it to the attention of the government in two years' time.

away when most of the discussion took place on this matter. But certainly my reading of the evidence that was taken and of the discussions that took place indicated to me that there was to be a review of the whole situation, not by the members of the Indian department but by the House of Commons.
I can say this, Mr. Chairman. I have been in western Canada during the last few days; and during my absence I have received letters from various chiefs in western Canada who are not at all satisfied with the situation under the act as at present amended. I feel that if the review is to be restricted to the members of the Indian department, such a review is worthless from the point of view of protecting the rights of the Indians in this country.
The Indian Act has been before the members of the department over the years. To say that any changes, alterations or suggestions as to improvement are to emanate from the members of that department certainly will hold out little hope that many beneficial changes will take place. Indeed, I have here a letter from a chief, written within the last few days, wherein he sets forth that various chiefs are even now meeting, or have been meeting within the last few days, with a view to making further representations. I speak of the descendants

speechtext: So there is.

-not by the members of the Indian department but by members of the House of Commons, with a view to bringing about changes and improvements.
I know that the experience of the hon. member for Essex West would go a long way in the convening of another committee to bring about the necessary changes that must be made. From my own experience I know there are in western Canada Indian tribes who have the right to ask for justice which, up to the present time, has been denied them. I think of the cases in which Indian tribes, within the last fifteen years, have been denied the right to take action against His Majesty the King. I know of one case that was taken-and successfully taken-arising out of highly improper conduct in connection with the handling of money belonging to the reserve. I refer to the Mistawasis case. A justice of the Court of King's Bench in Saskatchewan allowed substantial damages for the wrongs that had been done; and from that date on, no right of action has ever been granted to any Indian tribe in Saskatchewan that made application for a fiat that justice be done, so that action could be commenced.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member would not want to misinform the committee. That statement is not a fact.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
All right. I understand that statement is correct. I was the one who made application for the fiat; and that is fifteen years ago. From the time that action was taken in the Mistawasis case before Mr. Justice McLean in Saskatchewan, fiats have not been granted. But we do not have to worry about fiats any more; for in the next few days when the act is passed-if it is passed-through this parliament doing away with the need for a fiat, the rights of all His Majesty's subjects, whether Indians or others, will not be dependent upon the caprice of any minister as to whether or not action is to be commenced.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister at this moment and I say this. Will he consider carrying out the request of the Indian chiefs-and I think it has been brought to his attention on more than one occasion-for the setting up, with regard to these reserves where there are claims of injustices, a royal commission for the purpose

Indian Act
of investigating whether or not there is justice in the request of these Indians, to the end that every possible feeling of injustice on their part will be removed by a judicial or semi-judicial inquiry? If that was done, I think much improvement in morale would result.
During the period that the minister has been in office I know that he has brought the various Indian chiefs to Ottawa, that they have discussed the matter with him and with his departmental officials, and that improvements are taking place. But there remains in the hearts and the souls of many Indians throughout the western provinces an abiding feeling of injustice. Under treaty they turned over everything they had to Her Majesty Queen Victoria, and they feel that the promises that were made by her Britannic majesty's representatives have not been fully carried out. I feel that if such a course were followed by the minister it would go a long way towards removing that feeling which prevails among many of these bands and tribes, namely that injustices that have accumulated over the years have not been satisfactorily eradicated or removed or that compensation for wrongdoing has not been given. Realizing that the act as it is being amended today by this bill will remove some of the injustices, in all seriousness I ask the minister to give consideration to the appointment of a royal commission so that whatever other financial injustices may exist may be determined and proper compensation may be given to those affected.
This act has been in effect-I speak from recollection now-for approximately seventy years, with few changes. The revamping of this act has been an unusually difficult and trying job. It has required the co-operation not only of the committee of two or three years ago but of the departmental officials. It has received the co-operative assistance of the minister. But I feel that one thing still remains to be done. I feel that everything possible should be done to remove from the hearts and souls of Indians everywhere, particularly those in the western provinces- and of them only I speak-the feeling of having suffered what they believe to have been injustices.
I remember so well, in 1934, when the Indians gathered near Duck Lake on the sixtieth anniversary of the signing of the treaty that ceded those great western claims to Queen Victoria and her successors, Lord Tweedsmuir met with the descendants of those Indian chiefs, some of them sons of the chiefs who had been signatories to that treaty that gave to the British crown that great area extending from the western shores

of Hudson bay and thence to the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains. Those chiefs, some of whom were sons of the chiefs who were the signatories to that treaty, one after the other raised the question as to instances of what they believed to have been injustices for which they and their bands would be entitled to compensation. I remember so well that Lord Tweedsmuir, as His Majesty's representative, promised them in the name of His Majesty that any injustices and unfairness that may have existed would be removed. Of course he had to speak within the limits of his constitutional position. I make this appeal to the minister. Let us not only make this act work, but let us also do something to remove that feeling that does exist-and I think it rightly exists-that in too many cases, as a result of the law being what it is, and as contained within the Indian Act, promises that were made to these people, the aborigines on the western plains, have in fact not been carried out in accordance with justice and just dealing, as promised at the time the treaties were made.
I ask the minister again, has he given consideration now, since a new act is about to be passed, to the setting up of such a commission, free of and removed from the Indian department, judicial, if you like, in its nature, to the end that the claims for compensation, if they have any legal basis, will once and for all be determined by a judicial body, and, if there is any legal basis for the claims of these Indians, that compensation be given?
