speechtext: I do not want to create the impression that I am an expert on Indian affairs. As a matter of fact I do not know of any experts on Indian affairs in this house.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Thank goodness this is one department that has no experts.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: However, I do think that the impression that has been given by the hon. member for Lake Centre is not fair either to himself or to the members of the Indian administration. As I said, I do not know of any experts in the house, with probably one exception, namely, the minister himself who has within a very short period of time taken such a keen interest in the affairs of the Indians that he has grasped the situation among the Indians, as I see it, in a commendable way. I do believe that in fairness to the Indian administration, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Peace River, this matter is one primarily of administration. In that regard the Indian problems have largely, if not dissolved, at least lessened in the past few years. This

has happened, as the hon. member for Peace River has pointed out, since the committee was formed.
Under the able assistance of Mr. R. A. Hoey much was done to improve Indian affairs. I think that the Indians of this country, and the people generally, owe him a deep debt of gratitude. He has been succeeded by Major D. M. MacKay, who is now director of Indian affairs. He comes to the administration after many years in this work, and after having lived for some time among Indians on the west coast. He has done a remarkable job in improving Indian administration. I think we are very fortunate in Canada to have an administration of this type and an administration headed by a person of such integrity and ability.
Mr. T. R. L. Maclnnes has had many many years of experience. He is well versed in the history, lore and habits of the Indians, and has a great sympathy for their problems. I know that the hon. member for Lake Centre has, with me, a very high regard for his integrity and his ability.
That is correct.

I would not have it appear that there is any reflection whatever on the department heads. I could go on all through the department and point out individuals who have sacrificed considerably to be of service to the Indians.
There is another matter which has been brought up, and which I think should be referred to, namely, that we have not given the Indian an opportunity to appear before the committee. The committee formed in 1946 took as its theme that we were going about to help the Indians help themselves, and I think they have adhered strictly to that policy. We brought to Ottawa to appear before this committee Indians from all parts of Canada. When we could not get the Indians to agree we brought different factions from different provinces. In addition to that, a select group of the committee, ten in number, went down to the maritime provinces, and there heard every individual Indian who had anything to say on Indian affairs. I personally, and at my own expense, I may say, went out to the west coast to see how the Indians lived, to hear them and as much as possible to observe their habits and customs. I know, too, that the minister has travelled across this country hearing and seeing the Indians, and has tried to get a greater knowledge of their problems.
You will recall too, sir, that early in the session Indian representatives from every province in the dominion were brought to Ottawa, and they met with the minister in
Indian Act
closed conference to discuss the bill which is before the committee now. It may be argued that there were some there who were not representative. Well, those who have any knowledge of Indian affairs will realize that it is very difficult to get one person to represent any large group of persons, and it is no exception among Indians, but I feel sure, from the knowledge I have of the representatives who attended that conference, that the persons who were in attendance did truly represent the large majority, and by far the largest majority, of the Indians in the provinces from which they came. They were in conference for several days. They went over this bill, clause by clause. I was not in attendance myself. What I am saying is hearsay. They went over the bill clause by clause and voiced any objections that they might have, and these objections were brought before the committee of this house which has considered this bill, so that when it is said that the Indians have not been heard, it is not quite correct.

Mr. Chairman, I had the privilege of serving on the Indian committee for a number of years. While the redistribution in 1949 took away most of the Indians it was my honour to represent, I still take an interest in Indian affairs.
I entered the chamber too late to hear everything the hon. member for Lake Centre said; but from those few remarks I did hear it appeared to me he was suggesting that a claims commission should be set up.
That is right.

I do not wish at this time to go over the ground I covered before when speaking in the house. My remarks at that time were lengthy, and anyone who wir.hm to know what I said will find them record i 1 mi Hansard.
I still think however that if we are gomg to convince the Indians that we are giving them a new deal we will have to correct their thinking. If one argues with them he will find they still think, indeed they are positive, that we owe them something, and that we are keeping something back from them.
The minister has heard me say many times that the Manitoba Indians will quote what they were promised back in 1871. They continue to tell their families that these are the things the white man or the Queen Mother promised them, and that the obligation has not been fulfilled.
I have never thought in terms of a royal commission, but I do believe a claims commission such as that suggested by the hon.

Indian Act
member would be useful, so that whoever was placed in charge of it could get these matters straightened out once and for all. The Indian population is increasing, and as it does so there will be more who will believe that there has been an injustice.
I believe all hon. members realize it was necessary to revise the Indian Act. While I did not always get my own way in committee, I was content to accept the rule of the majority. I would have liked to see the Indians back here in Ottawa, so that I would have had the opportunity to talk with them and to ask them some questions. They, too, would have had the opportunity to ask questions. A majority in the committee however ruled to the contrary, and I feel one must abide by the decision of the majority.
To let hon. members know what I have in mind I should like to place on record a telegram I received. We were led to believe that when the Indians went home they were satisfied they had got everything their own way. This telegram addressed to me at the House of Commons states:
Informed special committee passed bill seventy-nine without incorporating recommendations from conference Indian representatives. If report true deeply regret and strongly protest such action. Urge reconsideration of contentious clauses during debate. Urge amendments suggested by conference be included. Consent of governed in principle concern.
That is from the Indian Association of Alberta, one of the men who were here to meet the Indian committee. I should have liked to see these Indians again. I did not have the opportunity to speak to the Indians from Manitoba. It is possible that, had they been here, we would not have got any further, but I believe that opportunity should have been given.
I shall not take more time in speaking on this occasion. There are one or two questions I should like to ask at a later time. We must realize however that the Indians have gone home and that they are still not satisfied. Some of my friends will say that we will never satisfy them. My reply however would be that we could go a long way toward meeting more of their grievances; and I think a claims commission would be one way of helping to straighten out their thinking which, it may be, is not always in accordance with the facts.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to speak at length now, because on a previous occasion I did discuss the matter more fully. I believe however there are some points which ought to be made before we proceed to discuss the bill in detail.

It is my view that in large measure the value of the bill will depend upon the general attitude in the minds of those administering the act. If the attitude is taken that the rights of the Indians ought to be extended, and that on all occasions they should be given the benefit of the doubt, then I believe the act will pretty well take care of itself. However if the opposite view is taken we shall require an exceptionally good piece of legislation to prevent considerable damage being done to the Indians.
To make it perfectly clear to those who may read my remarks that I am not suggesting in any way that those who are now administering the Indian Act are negligent or deficient in their general attitude, let me say at once that, so far as I can see, the present Indians branch has the right idea, and is working forward progressively. I believe that should be said.
Almost anyone must agree that the present bill is much superior to any bill of a similar kind presented to any Canadian parliament heretofore. I believe anyone who knows the facts must agree that the minister in charge of Indian affairs has far surpassed anyone charged with a similar responsibility in the whole history of the Dominion of Canada. As such he deserves the credit and honour due a man who discharges his duties in a statesmanlike manner. I believe history will give him credit for what he has already done, and what I believe he still will do.
Perhaps I should add that I am not alone in the opinions I express. A statement from the Alberta Indian Association, issued since the bill was published, states that the new Indian Act in the present revised form is an excellent piece of legislation. It points out that the government has made the most serious study of the Indians themselves, and seems genuinely interested in giving these people a charter that will ensure their steady progress and development.
In those sentiments I heartily concur. Yet I believe there are some words of warning which ought to be uttered on this occasion.
There appears to be a belief among a good many people that the day ought to come by and by when the whole matter of Indians can be' written off as finished business in Canada. People entertaining such views take the general point of view that we ought to integrate the Indians with the whites just as rapidly as we can. We might even have regulations to impose enfranchisement upon the Indians as one means of achieving that objective. Such people hold also that we should disintegrate and ultimately eliminate the reservation, and they have in mind certain

devices whereby that objective could be attained, even by using the present Indian Act.
Between me and the men who take that attitude there is a sharp and I might almost say violent opposition in point of view. I do not believe the day will ever come, at least in our time, when we can write off the Indian as finished business. If we are not to write him off as finished business we must make provisions for expanding our services to the Indian down to the latest generation. Once that principle is laid down and followed our whole approach to the Indian problem will change.
There .are certain rights which I believe the Indians possess. First of all, the Indian has a right to remain an Indian and to have his children and his children's children remain Indians to the latest generation if they so desire. There are certain reasons why this is the case.	Indians are very
religious. Their traditions go back through the millenniums. They do not want to see themselves disappear as Indians any more than the members of the tribe of Judah desire to see themselves cease to be members of the tribe of Judah. Those who understand the Indians know that they are just as tenacious in their feelings in this respect as are the descendants of Judah. No people, no officials can disregard that profound and far-reaching fact without doing violence to sacred beliefs among the Indians. If some day Indians outgrow those beliefs then the situation will be different. But as long as they maintain those beliefs which have been handed down to them by their fathers, we have a reality there, even though it may be an intangible reality, which we must not lightly treat.
The Indian has the right to have his reservation preserved inviolate as a place of refuge for his children and his children's children whenever those children may find themselves unable to compete successfully with non-Indians in the struggle for existence. Let us consider just how serious that can be in the fearful times through which we are going. Every hon. member knows that it is next to impossible today for the most qualified non-Indian to get employment if he is thrown out of employment at 65 years of age. A great many people, regardless of how skilful they may be, find it next to impossible to obtain employment when needed after 50 years of age. If we are going into that sort of thing it must be obvious that the Indian is going to be under a most serious disadvantage when he attempts to compete in the economy of the non-Indian.
Indian Act
To me this is a most solemn consideration, and I think all hon. members will agree with me. If the white man, the non-Indian, insists on so managing his affairs that there is little use for our own people after they are 45 or 50 years of age, he must realize that he has a responsibility toward the Indian which must be assumed. If we are going to indulge ourselves in the luxury of supporting a financial and economic system like that, we at least should see that the Indian does not have to pay the price.
The Indian has the right to remain out of our wars if he sees fit. We say that the Indian was born here, that he is a Canadian and therefore has a responsibility to defend this country. That is one point of view. But in most of the original treaties there was a stipulation that the white queen would never call upon the Indians to fight her wars. That was a sacred promise. We must take into consideration along with that fact the fact that these wars that we fight generation after generation are of our own making or the result of the economic system under which we choose to operate. That is known to all well-informed people. The Indian should not have to go and shed his blood to fight our wars.
The Indian has the right to the highest degree of training of every kind. Up to the present we have not begun to give the Indian that right. In only a very few cases scattered far and wide has there been even an approximation to doing that. Yet some people are thinking of pushing the Indians out into the stream of economic competition where they will have little or no chance at all. The boys and girls of even our race are going out into that stream of competition and are finding that at 45 or 50 years of age they are unable to compete successfully!
All we have to do is remember what happened during the depression when Canada had a million and a quarter of her people unemployed, not because they were not able to work, not because they were not willing to work, not because there was not a tremendous amount of work to do, but simply because we insisted on following a financial and economic system that made it almost impossible for men to get work under the best of circumstances. If we insist on keeping that financial system, how in the world can we justifiably expect the Indian to suffer for that?
The Indian has a right to adequate rehabilitation. It is too late now to train many Indians who are 45 or 50 years of age, even those of 25 years of age, but surely something ought to be done for these people. Until such time as we are positively certain

Indian Act
that Indians can be fully quaiiiied for participation in the economic struggles of our time it seems to me this right ought to bear a special cogency in our minds.
The Indian has a right to compensation for the injustices that have oeen done him in the past. The hon. member for Lake Centre, the hon. member for Peace River, the hon. member for Selkirk and a great many other hon. members have said things which indicate they are in general agreement with that statement. How are we going to give the Indians compensation for the harm that has been done them during the 150 years or so we have been in this country? The first thing we have to do is to find out what that harm has been and its impact upon the Indian of today. Therefore it becomes necessary to address ourselves to the problem of discovering the solution to this situation.
Some people say: Certain groups of Indians have no treaty rights, and therefore we have no further obligation to them. For example, I am told that a great many Indians in eastern Canada have not been fortunate enough to be treaty Indians while the Indians in the western provinces have become treaty Indians. There are people who say that because we did not sign any treaties with those Indians in the east they are not entitled to as fair consideration as our Indians in the west. I think such people overlook the important fact that our fathers had become a great deal more civilized by the time they dealt with the Indians of the west than their fathers were several generations before when they dealt with the Indians in the maritimes.
We talk about the Indians becoming civilized. The white man had to become civilized, and the average white man among us has a long way to go yet before he is really civilized if you take the word "civilized" to mean thoroughly prepared to co-operate with his fellows in obtaining the betterment of all, and that is the only sound definition of "civilized".
Some people say that the Indians have no special legal rights, and why bother about such Indians? I confess that such arguments seem to me quite unsound. The Indians' rights in my judgment result from the fact that America was the Indians' promised land. Maybe that does not mean as much to certain other members of the house as it does to me. Judging from the expressions on the faces of the members present I think however it does mean as much to them.
This land was their land. The land of both North and South America was the Indians'. They owned it by prior right. The

Indian settled here first and had been here for thousands of years before the whites ever came. We must never forget that. Then the white man came to this promised land of the Indian. He did not conquer the Indian. He negotiated with him as an equal. Then he killed the Indians' buffalo with his guns. He caught the Indians' fish with his advanced methods of fishing. He cut down and ruined the Indians' forests with his advanced methods of cutting them down. He burned them down by devices which he had and which the Indians either did not have, or else knew a whole lot more about how to take care of. He spoiled the Indians' pastures. He trespassed on the Indians' hunting and camping grounds. He dried up and polluted the Indians' rivers and streams; he fenced off the Indians' trails.
Every single step in that unhappy process rendered it more and more difficult for the Indians to survive. Will anyone seriously argue that the Indian was not establishing rights by indirect measure when all that was occurring? Will anyone seriously argue in his saner moments when he is no longer a politician that when the white man did all these things he did not assume a responsibility to the Indian which the white man's children should at least endeavour to discharge? As a result of all these things the white man did against the Indians, the Indian was left with inadequate means of adjusting himself to the white man's economic life. Generally speaking the white man did nothing about it at all except to beat the Indian whenever he could.
Beat?

Yes, beat. At this point let me read a short passage from this same document of the Indian Association of Alberta just to show what the white men have done. I am taking it right out of its context but it is appropriate. It is as follows:
And in the late 1800's, when Indians were being brought into treaty, both Indians and mixed bloods were offered land scrip in exchange for treaty rights. This scrip entitled the holder to crown lands, and of course was valuable. Unscrupulous whites cheated many an illiterate and simple Indian or "breed" out of his or her scrip by offering in trade a bottle of rotgut whiskey, a few yards of print or some gaudy trifles. And of course the victims kept on living with the band, for they couldn't do anything else. Eventually, in P.C. 1182, 1901, Hon. Clifford Sifton, minister of the interior, ruled that these people could be taken back into treaty, with the value of their squandered scrip to be deducted from their annuities. But Bill 79 states outright that no recipient of scrip or any of his descendants may be registered as an Indian.
That is painting an ugly picture in big broad splashes, is it not? Every member of this house who has any genuine contact

with the Indian situation at all knows that this kind of thing has occurred and occurs today. In my judgment there is only one way in which we can deal with this whole situation satisfactorily. That is by doing what I suggested the last time I spoke, namely, setting up two specific commissions. These commissions would not be set up under the Indian Act, but would be commissions which would work in co-operation with the department in administering the Indian Act. The first one would be an Indian claims commission that would probe into history, find out the facts, and then find out what the impact of those facts is upon the Indians today and what measures ought to be taken to reimburse or recompense the Indian so that his children may know that something was done at least in our generation to be fair to him.
Then we should have an Indian rehabilitation commission, as I suggested before. No Indian department could do this work. The personnel of the department are so overworked now that all you have to do is to look at them to see that that is so. You can step into the office of almost any one of these men and you will see that they are positively overworked. How in the world can men like that, burdened with thousands and thousands of administrative details for many of which they have no guide to follow, use the imagination and initiative which is necessary to enable them to adapt the Indians to the particular circumstances surrounding them? Let me give an illustration concerning the Indian reserve which I have the honour to represent. In our area there is a beet growing section for which there is need for a great number of beet workers. If the appropriate officials could come and train the Indians to be beet workers, as they could, as skilfully as the Indians of Caughnawaga have been trained to become steel workers, then as long as the beet sugar factories remained there the Indians would be assured of good jobs off the reservation every year. They would learn to be just as successful at that kind of work as the d.p.'s who come from Czechoslovakia, Poland, Hungary and other places, and fit right into that scheme and prosper among the beet fields. This is only an illustration; there must be countless instances from coast to coast in Canada. An Indian rehabilitation commission would undertake to discover these possibilities of training Indians to adapt themselves to the economic life surrounding them and in due time would make them a far happier and more useful people both to themselves and to us.
Indian Act
Indians of today have still other grievances. With all the other things we have done to the Indians our government now insists on taxing them on the income they make off the reserves. Numbers of my fellow members in the house seem to think that is all right, but to me it is positively revolting. We say to the Indian in effect that we simply defy him to adapt himself to conditions outside the reserve and make a success, but that if he does we will tax him for the privilege of doing so. I do not see how anyone can face with equanimity a proposition like that, it is so outrageous. Let us take the Caughnawaga people, for instance; suppose they are able to make a pretty good income off the reserve. They could return to the reserve and improve it; buy more land, do reforestation, restock the streams, and all that sort of thing. They could do it if they could take back to the reserve the income they earned elsewhere, but no; as soon as they make any money the white man steals it from them in taxes so they go back practically impoverished, just as the white man in general goes back to his home with a pay envelope altogether inadequate to meet his needs.
The situation thus confronting the Indian is quite hopeless. The white man insists on doing this also; or, if he does not exactly insist on it, there are indications in this legislation that he may do so! If an Indian does excel, if he establishes himself in a conspicuous manner as a success among the white men, the government might say, "Well, you have done very well. You can get along without assistance. We do not need to help you any longer. We will enfranchise you and turn you loose among the whites." It will not matter at all if that Indian's grandchild should not be as successful as he was. The grandchild may not be successful at all; nevertheless he will be enfranchised and to the end of time all the privileges and rights which were guaranteed to him as an Indian will be taken away because he had an ancestor who happened to be successful. Is that not almost unbelievable for intelligent men in 1951 to be contemplating? Yet that is the sort of thing presumably facing the Indians. They are very bright and keen, and though they do not talk very much about it they understand how serious it is. It fills them almost with dismay, all over the land.
I promised, Mr. Chairman, that I would not speak too long. I intend to keep that promise, but I want to say one further word which will perhaps offer a ray of hope. I want to project myself now into the minds of those men who say we have to get to the point somehow where we can write off these Indians, because if

Private Bills
we make it possible for them to multiply the first tiling we know we shall have millions of them and we shall not be able to take care of them. They think we are going to have more old age pensioners. Now that we are bringing the pensionable age down to 65, the first thing you know we will have to bring it down to 60, then to 55; and they want to know where in the world we are going to end. I realize men are thinking in such terms today; but let me assure people from coast to coast in Canada and the members of this house that if we would adopt a realistic financial system these worries would disappear at once. Then we would not ask where we were going to get the money to do all these things for the Indians, for our aged people, and others. We would ask whether we in Canada can produce the milk and the cream and the butter and the eggs and the meat and the lumber and the clothing and the fuel. Can we produce enough of those commodities to take care of all those who will be born to us and to the Indians? The answer must come back a thunderous "Yes". Well, all we have to do is adopt a financial system that will be realistic in respect to our productive capacity so the financial system will reflect the facts of our production. Then we shall have no cause for any anxiety as to our ability to advance the welfare of our Indians to the very end of time, or as long as the good Creator wills that v/e remain here as a free and independent people.
Now may I close with one more word of commendation to the minister. I cannot put into language, without seeming to overdo it, my admiration for the kind of work the minister has done during the last year; nor can I convey to the government all the appreciation it would be fitting to express. By reason of what it has done for the Indians, on paper at least, and by reason of the attitude I find in most of its members, I believe the Liberal party deserves high commendation. I think it stands unique in the history of Canada in its manner of treating our Indians.
With these few words, which I utter sincerely and from my heart, I shall conclude. I wish the minister greater and greater success and greater and greater vision. I wish the men of his department also greater vision; and I hope they will have a minister of finance before long who will be able to make the financial system reflect the physical realities of Canada.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words with respect to clause 1 of this bill. This is a case which I feel deserves the support of this house, and I for one not only intend to vote for this bill, but I feel that all hon. members should vote for it.
I shall take just a moment to indicate in brief the circumstances. This is a case of a woman living in England-she is still there. A Canadian soldier went overseas during world war II and married her. They lived together while they were both in England, and they had one child, a son. After the end of the war the soldier appears to have deserted his English wife and returned to Canada. For a number of years she did not hear from him or about him in any way. Later she learned that he was back in Mont -real and had married again.
Some time after this second so-called marriage the second wife discovered that her husband was already married to a lady in England, and so she obtained an annulment of her marriage in a Quebec court. That annulment was granted on December 19, 1946. When the lady in England learned of the situation she took steps to get a divorce from her Canadian husband. The woman who became the so-called second wife appeared as the chief witness for the deserted wife. She appeared at the Senate and gave evidence that she, not knowing that this man had been previously married, went through a form of marriage with him, and subsequently lived with him. On the basis of that evidence the Senate committee had no hesitation in approving of this divorce.
This is one of those human tragedies about which we all feel very sad. It is unfortunate that nothing can be done to force this man to contribute to the support of his and his wife's child in England, but surely the least we can do for this English girl is to see to it that she gets this divorce. This is one case where I felt I should not mention any of the names involved. I do call upon the house to support this bill.

I should like to say just a word or two about this bill. I support the views of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in suggesting that this house should pass this bill. However, there are one or two things I should like to say about it. The point I would like to make now I

do not want to be regarded as any reflection upon the committee of the other place that heard this evidence.
I notice that the acting chairman was Senator Fogo. I understand that he is rather an outstanding barrister, and perhaps-
I would not say that.

I do not know. There may be other opinions. That is my understanding. Perhaps I will have to take his authority for it. But there is one place in the evidence in which the marriage record-that is the second marriage record-is presented, and the acting chairman says: "It is not a record of marriage, because it was not a marriage at all, but a form of marriage which she went through."
I am one member in the house who has performed a good many marriage ceremonies; and I have never performed one yet, and had it registered, where I did not feel pretty certain that the marriage, as performed, was more than a form of marriage. It may be a technical point, but I would point out, as was pointed out in the evidence, that this certificate of marriage was also registered in the superior court, district of Montreal. If anyone wished to apply to the superior court for an abstract of that certificate, he would have proof enough that this woman was married to the man, even though he had no right to marry a second time.
During the first world war I was called up under a certain category for military service. It happened that I was married, and should not have been called up in the first category. When I saw the authorities I told them I was quite prepared to go into the services at the proper time. However they wanted proof of my marriage, and so I submitted to them-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHILDREN OF PENSIONED WIDOWS, BURIAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this amendment to the Pension Act. Under this amendment it is proposed, among other things, to provide that widows of members of the forces with children will be able to be paid on the basis of schedule B for orphans; in other words, that their pension for their children will be doubled. Under schedule B the payment for the first child is $228; for the second child, $180 and for each subsequent child, $144. On the basis under which they are being paid now, that of the orphaned child, there will be $456 for the first child, $360 for the second child and $288 for the third child. That is doubling the amount which will be payable under that clause.
The point that I want to raise with the minister is this. I do not see anything in the bill which gives any increase to an orphaned child. There are numbers of children who are orphans of members of the forces and they are receiving, according to the schedule which I have just read, $38 a month in the case of one orphan or $68 where there are two. I do not see anywhere anything to indicate that this payment is being increased.
[Mr. Speaker.!
It seems to me that if we are doubling the amount that is payable to a dependent child, certainly we should be doing something with respect to the orphaned child. I would ask the minister to comment on that feature and tell us just why we should be doubling the one without giving any increase to the other, as I read the act.
The other matter that I wish to comment on is that of education for children of the veterans. Under this act we are proposing to continue the payment up to twenty-one years of age where the child is able to absorb the education, is passed as being able to do so, and requires further education. That is all to the good. But again I say that in the case of orphaned children we are doing nothing under these amendments to the act, as I read them. If I am mistaken in this, I hope the minister or his parliamentary assistant will correct me.
It seems to me that we in Canada owe a duty to these orphans of the men in our forces. It seems to me that we owe these orphans an opportunity to receive as good an education as they can absorb or are capable of attaining. If their fathers had returned to Canada we would have provided, under the veterans charter, for their training in specialized trades or they could have had up to four or five years in university. Where there are orphaned children, it seems to me that we should be prepared to give them an opportunity equal to that which would have been available to their fathers had they returned to this country. I see nothing in this act which provides for that.
I think it is a disgrace in this country if we are going to leave orphaned children of members of our forces in the position that that they will not have every opportunity of obtaining the best education that it is possible for them to have. I do not see any provision made for that under the act. I should like the minister to comment on those two matters before we give second reading to the bill.

I should like to support the amendment. As a member of the committee may I say the fact that a majority of that committee favoured the government's position does not mean very much, except that a majority of the committee were simply following the minister's direction.
As I understand it, the purpose of this bill is to gradually encourage the Indians to become enfranchised and to assume their position as democratic citizens in Canada. One of the ways in which this can be achieved is by giving them such responsibility as they are capable of discharging.
One of the criticisms I have had is that in more than 70 clauses of the bill the responsibility rests upon the minister or the governor in council without consultation with the bands or with any of the Indian representatives. If we are aiming to educate these people, to teach them to assume responsibility, we must give them some responsibility and not place these matters entirely in the hands of the minister or the governor in council, without even consulting with the band or with the people concerned.

In this particular instance it would seem to me that it would be quite logical to consult the band in the case of people who have probably spent their lifetime on the reserve. I feel they should not be removed at the whim of the minister or the department, and particularly if there was opposition to that on the part of the band. subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having seconded the proposed amendment, I should like to say a word in support of it. Section 4 as at present worded gives to the governor in council authority to declare by proclamation that this act or any portion thereof, except sections 37 to 41-and only five sections are excepted'-shall not apply to any Indian, or any group or band of Indians. As I recall, sections 37 to 41 are those dealing with the surrender of lands. All matters outside the scope of those five sections can be dealt with by the governor in council by proclamation, if section 4 in its present form is accepted.
This means that the very matter of the status of an Indian can be dealt with by proclamation, without the consent of the Indian. The very existence of a band, their status as a band of Indians, and their continuance or otherwise as a band of Indians can be dealt with by the governor in council by proclamation, without consent of the band.
We have heard in committee, and in the house before the bill went to committee, that one of the efforts being made-and a very praiseworthy one indeed-is to achieve equality of status for the Indians; and not only to put it into legislative form but to convince the Indians that that is our intention. Indeed it is suggested that, by our example, and through the means of this legislation, we should encourage the Indians to assume equality of status with us, so that eventually they might graduate into full citizenship and absolute equality with the white man.
Surely it goes without saying that no municipality in Canada would give consent to having its status interfered with or changed by proclamation of the governor in council, without the consent of the municipality; and I am sure the House of Commons would not consent to any interference with its status on that basis. I very much doubt if the house would consent to authorizing the governor in council to make a proclamation changing the status of a white individual, without his consent. In most cases, so far as white people are concerned, before any change in status can be brought about, and before any penalties for breach of legislation

can be imposed, or anything of that sort, legislation which must receive the sanction of parliament is required.
Here, however, it is not legislation; it is a proclamation of the governor in council. In view of the fact that there are so many administrative matters which must also be dealt with under this statute, I think it is quite acceptable to have the matter dealt with by the governor in council, and not to require legislation before anything can be done; but if we are going to place that tremendous power in the hands of council, namely the power of changing the status of individuals, groups or bands of Indians, then surely we must put in a safeguard that the change must be made with the consent of the Indian or band concerned. That is the effect of the amendment.
It does not make it impossible to make these proclamations. The section, if amended as suggested, would read that the governor in council may, with the consent of the Indian or band concerned, by proclamation declare that this act or any portion thereof, except sections 37 to 41, shall not apply to any Indians or any group or band of Indians, and so on. So it does not take away any of the ultimate power of the governor in council, nor does it in any way abridge the things that may be done by proclamation of the governor in council.
All it does is to require that before these things which affect the very status of Indians, whom we say we are trying to place on a basis of equality, can be done, this consent by all concerned must be obtained. I appeal to hon. members who, I am sure, are desirous of creating in the Indians a sense of equality, to give to the Indians some control or some say in their own affairs, and to require that their consent must be obtained before any change in their status can be brought about by proclamation by the governor in council.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
This is one of the sections to which I referred in a general way when I spoke before six o'clock, and pointed out that in the Indian Act there were powers which, if used by an administration genuinely interested in the welfare of the Indian, could be instruments of benefit, but which, if they were used by an administration aiming to hurt the Indians, could become instruments of intimidation.
In effect, as I understand it, this section means that the department could excommunicate a band of Indians-and I use that word, not in its religious sense, but as it would be envisaged in connection with the operation of the act. Consequently if Indians, let us say on the Blood Indian reserve, which I have the honour to represent, became self-
Indian Act
assertive, or endeavoured to insist upon their rights in certain respects, as time goes on officials could say, "You boys had better be good, or we will bring section 4 on your heads." That is precisely the possibility involved in this section, as I understand it.
I believe it was pointed out in committee and, as I recall, the minister, as well as officials in his department, assured us that a section almost identical with this one had been in the act from the earliest time. However the Indians had never known it was there and consequently were not greatly concerned. It was said that all through the years, since it was first put into the act, it has never been used as an instrument of intimidation. Perhaps that is correct; but it is no proof that at some time it might not be used as an instrument of intimidation. We know there are certain Indians who are quite outspoken. For instance the Six Nations are outspoken, and in that they are not doing anything more than their forefathers told them to do, through traditions passed down to them through the years.
If the Indians are to become the selfreliant, courageous and outspoken people we hope they will become, and if they are to enjoy the freedoms we enjoy, then certainly they should not be put in a position where they can be intimidated through a section of this kind.
I think I have expressed clearly the way this appeals to the Indians. I believe it will be found that the Six Nations Indians are very much afraid that this section will be used in exactly the way I have indicated. As I said in committee, the department would not lose any material advantage by accepting the amendment which has been suggested. I believe if they did lose any flexibility of action in the administration of the act, through the inclusion of those words, they would gain in confidence and good will of the Indians to an even greater extent.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word, not so much as to the merits of the amendment, because others are more competent to do that, but rather to point out that we did have a debate on this subject before it went to committee some weeks ago. At that time I believe it was stressed by the minister, and I am sure in perfect sincerity, that what we were wishing to do, among other things, was to raise the status of these fellow citizens many of whom, incidentally, had served their country so well in wartime, and who were therefore entitled to consideration of their status.

Indian Act
The bill went to a committee and it has now come back to us here. Many of us were [DOT] not members of that committee. Reasons which seem to me to be most convincing have been given from this side for this amendment. If I remember correctly, the minister said that when the bill was before the committee this point had been raised and the committee had voted against it; that that was the government's view and they had not changed it. That seems to me to be an odd state of affairs. There are many on both sides of the house who have not had the benefit of hearing the discussion before the committee and surely we are not going to be left in a position where the matter is going to be voted on just because there is a majority without anyone on the government side undertaking to answer the arguments which have been made.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I regret that I did not make it clear in my explanation that I had discussed this particular section fully on second reading and gave them all the reasons which I believe I could give now as to why this section should remain in the bill. This section has been in the act since 1880, and, as the hon. member for Rethbridge has said, it did not cause concern to the Indians until the past few months when the matter was raised by some hon. members opposite.
The section is designed to aid in the flexible administration of Indian affairs so that the Indians may have the benefit of being removed from some of the restrictions in the act. If you did not have a section of this kind you would not be able to relieve the Indians from some of the restrictions unless the act was brought back to the house and it was done by way of amendment so that a particular section would not apply to a particular band. This is a salutary provision in the interest of the Indian and will be used for that purpose.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I accept the answer of the minister which I believe is given in absolute sincerity, that this section is intended to be used for the benefit of the Indian. The minister's answer seemed to be based on the assumption that we were moving to strike this section from the act. No such thing has been suggested. It is admitted that there must be flexibility. I stated specifically that we were not trying to strike out this section because then you would have to have new legislation each time you wanted to make some change. I admitted specifically that it was probably necessary for administrative flexibility to do many of the things that are contemplated to be done by proclamation of the governor in council.

The point of the amendment is not to strike out this section so as to make it necessary to have legislation to bring about any change. The point of the amendment is merely to require the consent of the band or the Indians affected before a proclamation is issued. The minister's answer has not dealt with that point at all. His answer has dealt with a situation based on the assumption that we are attempting to remove the section from the act, which of course is not so. We are merely attempting to ensure that the people whose welfare will be affected, whose status is going to be changed by the proclamations which are contemplated, must first give their consent.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Will the minister state how in his opinion the adoption of this amendment will interfere with the carrying out of the objectives of this bill?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is a very simple matter to deal with. As the committee knows, as the house knows from the discussion on second reading, and as the special committee knows, the Indians have not been unanimous on many sections of this bill nor are they unanimous on how the Indian affairs branch should administer particular matters. Everyone here knows that the opinion of a band council of this year may not be the opinion of a band council next year. If you take the sense of a band at any given moment it may not be the sense that would be shown the following day.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: That is true of the Canadian electors.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Quite so. As the
committee knows, in dealing with band affairs and Indian affairs a final decision must be made by someone as to what is in the interests of the Indians under all the circumstances. The power to make that decision is vested in parliament, and by the Indian Act is vested partially in the minister and partially in the governor in council. The final decision in these matters must rest in those hands rather than, in some cases, in the hands of the band council or of the individual Indian.
In some cases the sections give authority to the minister to do certain things with the consent of the band council. In other cases he may do certain things without the consent of the band council. I cannot recall a case, except in the surrender clauses, where the consent of the band is necessary. But certain privileges are vested in the band council, certain authority is vested in the minister, and certain authority in the governor in council.
If the time should come when a band would be benefited under certain circumstances by

the action of the governor in council taken under this section then I think parliament would hold the governor in council responsible if he did not exercise his judgment at that time as to what was in the interests of the band.
I do not want to precipitate a debate on later sections, but I might mention that this is the section which might be used to alter the liquor regulations which are covered by sections 95 to 100. It might very well be in those cases that one would obtain the consent of the band council, but as I have said at any given moment a decision may have to be made in the interests of the band and, since the responsibility for making those decisions is vested here, we shall have to have the right to make them.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: All the minister has told us is that in the opinion of his department the Indians at no time can be trusted to know what is best for them.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I said nothing of the kind.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: The minister has indicated that the minister or the governor in council must under all circumstances decide that they know better than the Indians affected what is in their best interests. How in the world does the minister expect the Indians to become independent and responsible citizens so long as he refuses them the right to decide what is in their best interests under any given circumstances?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: The provisions in the bill which give authority to the Indians and to the band council to exercise certain powers are the sections under which the band and the Indian may exercise those powers. If he exercises those and shows discretion in doing so-I know most of them are doing this at the moment-if he continues to learn the practices of democracy, we hope and believe that ultimately he will be not only ready but willing to accept the responsibilities for a much greater portion of self-government. Until that time there must be a division of authority among the minister, the governor in council, the band and the Indian.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I do not think the minister has appreciated the point we have tried to make. The amendment merely seeks to safeguard the welfare of the Indian. Before any proclamation is issued that affects the status or welfare of individual Indians or bands, it is asked that those Indians or bands must be consulted and give their consent. The minister has given an example. He says that section 4, subsection 2, might be used
Indian Act
to change the application of the liquor laws by exempting a certain band or group of Indians from the provisions of the bill. If one thing has been obvious in the consultations which members have held with Indians and with bands of Indians, it is that they are greatly concerned lest they should be subjected to wide-open liquor laws. Admittedly that is a question on which opinions vary considerably from band to band. It must surely therefore be a question which could most properly be dealt with in consultation with the band concerned. I understand that some bands feel now that they should be placed on a basis of absolute equality with white citizens. Other bands, as the minister has pointed out in his notes of the conference which he held with the Indians, feel that they should have a midway position, and there are others still where the majority feeling of the band is that they do not want any liquor on their reserves. They do not want their people allowed to buy liquor and they do not want the white man to be allowed to sell liquor to them. It is a case where opinion varies widely.
Surely therefore we should not give to the governor in council blanket authority to change the Indian Act with respect to liquor laws without the requirement that he consult first with the band and make the change only with the band's consent, in, effect if the band first requests it, which would of course imply their consent. That is all the amendment seeks to do, not to take away from the governor in council the ultimate power to exempt a band from the specific provision of the bill by proclamation,, but merely to ensure that that power is only exercised with the consent of the band concerned,. I think the example which the minister himself gave is a most powerful example to reinforce the proposition that the band's consent must be obtained before these proclamations are issued.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I hope the minister has helped other people more than he has helped me because I am still in great difficulty. When the minister began his remarks I thought he was really going to take the position that there was such a vacillation of feeling backwards and forwards that you could not, to use the words I think he used, be sure that an expression of opinion you got one day would be valid the next. The hon. member for York South answered that fairly well, but then the minister to my surprise went on and apparently made it quite clear that I was quite wrong in taking that point from him because he went on to explain that in certain cases they did act on consent.

Indian Act
Indeed he surprised me still further by saying, if I got his words right, that in the case of any question, of liquor, which I would imagine would be one of the most difficult and important involved, they might very well ask the consent of the band. That seemed to me to take the ground right from under the argument I thought he was making because he did not stick to what I thought was his first point, that you really could not get a consent that would stick. He does not maintain that point nor does he take the position that you must consult with the band only as to things that are rather unimportant- because surely the liquor question is not unimportant. Therefore I am really left quite at a loss, particularly in view of the explanation of the hon. member for Kamloops that this is only a minor restriction, to know what the argument is that the minister is making.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: After listening to the discussion on the amendment, it would appear to me that the minister does not want to agree to it because it is pretty obvious that he himself wants to do something that is going to be disagreeable to the Indians, or he would consent to it.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: That is the only conclusion one can draw.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Bosh.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
That is the only possible conclusion one can draw, because if he cannot get the consent of the band then it is obviously against their wishes. What would he possibly want to do against the wishes of the band that leads him not to agree to the amendment? What, for instance, would he want to do that would be so drastically against the Indians that he could not get their consent to do so? The matter of the liquor law is pretty important. The minister made the statement that they would probably get the consent of the band to make any change so far as that is concerned. In my estimation that is probably one of the most important parts of the whole act. In the case of some reserves it is more important than others. In some reserves he would not have any trouble getting the consent of the band to take the band out from under the act with respect to the liquor laws. In other cases it would be very difficult for him to do so. Would the minister suggest that he would want to do so against the wishes of the band? That is the only obvious conclusion we can draw.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was not a member of the special committee, but section 25 does not appear to be quite right the way I see it. Ownership of property has always been considered a very sacred thing. subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: This is the case, Mr. Chairman, of an Indian who transfers to another band, or something like that, and ceases to be entitled to live on the particular reserve. He has made improvements on his land, erected buildings, and of course is entitled to receive compensation for them. The Indian Act, however, does not provide for anyone holding land on a reserve except a member of that band, with one exception which you will see later. Therefore his transfer rights are limited to persons who can take land on that reserve. If he is unable to sell the land within six months the provision is that the land will revert to the band, who will hold it and perhaps later dispose of it to some other Indian; but, that having been done, that the band funds should recompense him for the improvements he has put on the land.

He should be entitled to

This section may have
been meant as a protection to the Indians, but surely by this time they have come of age and should be capable of carrying on their own negotiations. I would like the minister to give the committee a little enlightenment on that point.

speechtext:
What about property
held by the Indian outside the reserve? Oan the minister appoint executors to administer estates which contain holdings not within the reserve proper?

The minister

speechtext: Do I understand the effect of sections 42 and 43 is that Indians themselves may not make wills at all?

Where do you

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at section 45 he will see that the opening words are: "Nothing in this act shall be construed to prevent or prohibit an Indian from devising or bequeathing his property by will". subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Is it the practice in dealing with the estates of Indians under this and succeeding sections to deal with them in conformity with the laws of the province in which the property is situate, or is a standard practice followed throughout the dominion? The thought behind my question is that
Indian Act
if we are eventually to make Indians absolutely equal with us, sharing the same citizenship, the time will come when in respect to these matters of wills, succession to property and so on they will be subject to provincial law. So I am wondering if the administration of this and subsequent sections is now in accordance with the law of the province in which the property is located.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: We take our legal advice, of course, from the deputy minister of justice, who advises us on the particular points. The general rule is that we follow the common law in the province concerned. My hon. friend has raised a question, however, that is not settled in the Indian affairs branch. It may well be that we shall soon have to adopt a uniform practice throughout the dominion or, alternatively, have all these matters dealt with in provincial surrogate courts under provincial law; and I must say I am studying that at the moment.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: If a recommendation will be of any assistance at this time I would like to express the personal opinion that the move should be toward bringing these things under the same system in effect in the province so that there will be no eventual problem and no adjustments required in that regard.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I think that is logical, and we are looking at it in that light.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Is it true that in his will an Indian may not provide that his widow shall have a life lease on his land and property, and that it shall go to a son or daughter, as the case may be, on the death of the widow?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: That is a rather interesting point of law. It relates to the right an Indian has in land under his location ticket. That is not the full right of a fee simple, as we know it in Ontario, for example; and it has been suggested that since the Indian has what is in effect a right somewhat less than that, he may not be able to establish a life interest but can only establish a permanent interest the same as his own. I believe the particular point my hon. friend has in mind actually arose because of the unusual will in that case. I would prefer to put my answer this way, that we are trying to find a method by which Indian wills and the disposition of Indian lands will be comparable with the provincial registry laws, as the hon. member for Kamloops suggests, or something akin to that, so there will not be a distinction.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
First of all I have to ask the minister a question because

Indian Act
I am not as familiar with this act as I should be. Section 45 (3) states:
No will executed by an Indian shall be of any legal force or effect as a disposition of property until the minister has approved the will or a court has granted probate thereof pursuant to this act.
There may be some qualification of those words I do not know about; but assuming that a court has granted probate, notwithstanding that has the minister all the powers contained in section 46?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. The minister may direct that probate of a will be proceeded with through the surrogate court. If he does that he divests himself of any control over the ordinary administrative processes in that estate except as it relates to land on a reserve, because a will cannot take effect to transfer land on a reserve without the minister's consent, since the minister must sign all transfers whether of land willed or sold or otherwise.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Then may I assume that there is a section somewhere else in the act providing that the effect of a court granting probate is what the minister has just said, in other words that he will not have all the powers contained in section 46?

speechtext: Just under what circumstances would the minister likely be called upon to give consent for the court to exercise jurisdiction?

On section 46-Minister may declare will void.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I am not for
the moment saying whether section 46 is right or wrong; but it seems to me that we may as well face the fact that we are really just taking away any rights of any kind. I go on to section 47 because an appeal is provided for there. But how realistic is it to talk about an appeal with regard to the people we are talking about and whom we deal with in the words used in section 46? First let me read one or two subsections of section 46 to show how utterly illusory their rights are. You can hardly use the word "rights" with regard to them. I should like to read from the beginning of the section:
46. (1) The minister may declare the will of an Indian to be void in whole or in part if he is satisfied that-
Then I go on to paragraph (c):
(c)	the terms of the will would impose hardship on persons for whom the testator had a responsibility to provide,
(d)	the will purports to dispose of land in a reserve in a manner contrary to the interest of the band or contrary to this act,-
That seems to me to be absolutely wide open. Then finally:
(f) the terms of the will are against the public interest.
My comment, Mr. Chairman, is that provisions of that kind seem to me to be utterly repugnant to the declared intention, as I recall it, of the minister when he spoke to us first about this act. We would not treat children in that way.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend has overlooked the fact that the minister has been constituted a court under the previous section. This section in a general way provides jurisdiction in the minister comparable to that of a surrogate court judge or a supreme court judge in any action which might be brought with respect to a will. That does not answer the one particular question about the interests of the band; because there you interject a thing which would not be present in a lawsuit between non-Indians. But my hon. friend must remember that band councils and bands feel strongly at times about the disposition of land on their reserve. There are many reserves where all the land is allotted, where the allotments have been held by families going through several generations, and the thoughts of land tenure which are common to most of us

here are held by those Indians. But there are other reserves where the thought of allotment itself is opposed today and where, if there is a limited allotment, and if an Indian in his will purports to dispose of that land in a manner quite contrary to the commonly-accepted policy of that band, it might be in the interests of harmony and good relationship, and perhaps not affect really the interests of the heirs, to have this power which would not be exercised unless there were all these circumstances I have described.
I agree that it is repugnant to most ideas that we ourselves entertain; but my hon. friend will have to accept my word for it that there is a great deal of opinion that the band council should have the sole word as to any lands on a reserve; and many band councils today insist that no will be looked at and approved of by the minister until they have looked at it to see whether it affects the land tenure on that reserve.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS

What I have to say really
applies to all three subsections of section 66. Is there any safeguard to make sure that, if band funds are expended for these general benevolent purposes, Indians will not be deprived of benefits which they might hope eventually, at any rate, to receive under the general social security laws of the country? What I have in mind is this. Perhaps the answer will be self-evident, and perhaps I should therefore put it rather in the way of a suggestion for the future. Now that social security legislation is being made of universal application, but yet there are still means tests preserved in some of our social security legislation, as the Indians are brought along to a position of equality with the white man and, as I hope before long, are made the recipients of old age pensions, I would hope that the use of band funds for benevolent and charitable purposes and to look after the sick and the indigent and so on, that is provided for under this section will not in any way complicate the situation with respect to the means test; in other words, I hope it would not be counted as part of the income of an Indian for the purpose of disqualification for any social security benefits that he might otherwise be entitled to.

Section 72, paragraph (g), provides for medical treatment and health services to Indians. At this time I should like to commend the minister, his department, and also the special committee which has been acting for some time on behalf of our Indians.
In connection with the treatment and health services for our Indians, I should like to mention that in my home city of North Battleford, on the North Battleford airport, we have a splendid hospital that is entirely for Indian patients from the reserves of, I think, the Meadow Lake constituency and the constituency of The Battlefords. I should like to read into the record with respect to this hospital an item of Mrs. C. Wetton in the Star-Phoenix of April 20, 1951. Mrs. Wetton is special correspondent of the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix and also an authority on Indian history in our part of the province. This article carries the dateline North Battleford, August 22, 1876, and reads:
. . . and the third day of the Fort Carlton treatymaking :
"I have spoken much to you. Now I wish to hear the voices of your chiefs, or of those chosen to speak for you."
Governor Morris paused before the assembled tribesmen.
Poundmaker arose, to deliver an impassioned plea for aid for his people in the great task confronting them as they turned their footsteps to the white man's way of life, pleading at its close. "The children yet unborn, I wish you to treat them in like manner, as they advance in civilization like the white man. This is the voice of the people."
"I have heard the voice of the people," said the governor. "Those that come after us in the government, will think of your children, as we think of you."
How that pledge, so solemnly entered into in those far-away days at Fort Carlton is being fulfilled, is the story of the Indian hospital here.
It is a story of selfless endeavour; of men and women with wide experience, working in unison under the superintendency of Dr. P. W. Head for a better and fuller life for the descendants of those treaty makers; of the application of the latest in medical and surgical techniques, and nursing skills to the improvement of their health standards; and

of kindly guidance, in abundance, that has achieved more for the Indians here than anything else in their long story.
Indians are not demonstrative. But eagerly, now, they are seeking its benefits. No longer do they regard it as merely a government hospital for the Indians. "It is our hospital," they would have the world know.
At the last conference held here in Ottawa, called by the minister, there were two Indians down from my constituency, one chief Favel, representing the Queen Victoria protective association of Indians, and the other John Tootoosis, who is president of the Saskatchewan association of Indians. They advised me at the conclusion of their conference that they thought much good would come out of the conference and that it would be something for the betterment of the Indians of the future in the whole of Canada. After speaking to our two chiefs who were down I came to the conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that Bill No. 79 is the Magna Carta of our Indians.

I am sure we all agree, Mr. Chairman, that this bill is not perfect, but I must say that I myself feel it is as nearly perfect as we can make it in our first attempt to amend the Indian Act.
Subsection 2 of section 86 is what I consider to be the most vital part of the Indian Act. I refer to the right to vote or the right not to vote. I must say that this is the only section in which I found myself in complete disagreement with the minister. He himself holds very strong views on this matter, and I respect him for it. On the other hand, I feel that there is only one way in which the Indians will be able to bring before parliament effectively their desires of any worthwhile amendments to this legislation in due course. That will be done by virtue of the faot that they will have a vote. I have been long enough in politics, Mr. Chairman, to realize that people without a vote do not really have a great deal of power when they speak to a member of parliament. On the other hand, I notice that since the province of British Columbia gave the vote to Indians in provincial elections there has been decidedly a great deal more interest taken in Indian affairs by the members of the provincial legislature, and indeed by the government of the province of British Columbia.
This may be the only time I shall speak in the debate, and in doing so I should like sincerely to congratulate the minister upon the extremely fine job he has made of this revision of the Indian Act. He was not a member of the special committee which sat in 1946, 1947, and 1948. But I must say, as was pointed out today by the hon. member for Essex West, that he certainly outstripped us all in a very short time with his intense application to the job. It is my view that the Indians of Canada are most fortunate in having a man of his capacity to look after their interests at this time, when the act is before parliament for amendment.
In my lifetime I have had a unique experience with Indians and with the officials of the Indian affairs branch. My experience extends over a period of more than thirty-five years. I have had many business dealings with the department, both before coming to Ottawa as a member of parliament and since that time. I can only say that in all that time, both as an outsider and as a member, I have always received the fullest co-operation from the officials. I feel they are doing a wonderful job in the administration of Indian affairs. I would express to them and to the minister on behalf of a very large number
Indian Act
of Indians in my riding our thanks for and appreciation of the work done on behalf of those Indians.
While I hesitate to do so, I feel I must move, as I did in committee-
That subsection (2) of section 86 be deleted.
It seems to me that in subsection- 1 we recognize the claim by the Indians to exemption from taxation. And yet, at least in my opinion, in subsection 2-perhaps the minister will not agree with this-we ask the Indian to barter his right to the exemption for the privilege of voting in a federal election. That is something which I feel is fundamentally and basically wrong.
We inquire why this is done, and the minister say-s he does not want to set up a special category of Indians. It -seems to me there are about one hundred Indians in reserves in Canada-and I give that figure only as a rough guess-who are earning taxable incomes, or incomes that would be exempt under our present legislation. I would be very pleased to have the minister correct me if I am wrong. In other words we are disfranchising -about 125,000 people, or at least making it difficult for them, and asking them to waive -some of their rights, in order *that the Department of National Revenue here in Ottawa may collect some revenue from about one hundred Indians.
Let me point out that there are a great many people in Canada who do not pay income taxes. I look at one of our greatest provinces and realize that in it there are probably 200,000 farmers who enjoy the right to vo-te, who enjoy the privilege of receiving $40 a month old age pension, -and a-11 the amenities and other privileges enjoyed by white people; perhaps I should name the province of Quebec where there are -perhaps another 200,000 farmers who pay the sum total of $50,000 in income tax, or about 25 cents each per year; yet we give them all these rights.
In order to go ahead and collect from one hundred Indians who might or might not have taxable incomes, the government says, "You must give away these fundamental rights"-rights which we have already acknowledged under subsection 1. We ask them to give away the rights they would enjoy under this legislation, in exchange for the privilege of voting.
I do not think this has been explained to the average Indian-because, after -all, not many of them have much knowledge of or familiarity with the workings of the Department of National Revenue. Most of them do not realize that the greater proportion of the money they receive from their reserves will be in the form of capital, and would not be taxable. I do not think we have ever explained to those people that money -coming

Indian Act
in from oil or timber is a capital receipt and, as such, would not in any case be subject to income tax.
At least half the Indians in Canada'will be afraid to sign this waiver in order to gain the right to vote because they will feel that they are losing something. As I said in committee, it seems to me we are straining at a gnat in an effort to collect income tax from perhaps one hundred Indians.
If there is any flagrant abuse of exemptions from taxation, by people opening up large manufacturing establishments on Indian reserves, then that might become something-in the nature of a racket. I could then understand the minister's concern about something that might develop through time. So far as I know, however, that has not yet developed. Even if it has, perhaps we could go ahead and say that we would put a ceiling of $5,000 on the tax exempt income of an Indian on a reserve. Perhaps that would be reasonable.
On the other hand, if a business bringing in half a million dollars a year is developed, I am sure the Minister of National Revenue or the Minister of Finance could not resist the temptation of moving in and securing some of that revenue. It seems to me that this subsection would disfranchise Indians, perhaps because of their lack of knowledge of the manner in which the Income Tax Act applies, and that all this would be done to catch only a few Indians. This in my view is fundamentally wrong.
I hope that if the amendment is turned down tonight, it may be considered again in two or three years, when we see how the arrangement works out.
