Mr. Chairman, it is with regret that, entering the debate for the first time, I find I must oppose the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I feel however that in this instance we should place our views on record in connection with the amendment proposed by him.
I am going to vote against his amendment, and for two reasons, the first of which is purely technical. At the last session of parliament when amendments were made to the Dominion Elections Act a certain principle was accepted. My understanding is that at that time we set up, as a matter of law, the condition under which Indians as such, under the Indian Act, were entitled to vote at dominion elections. Through our own inadvertence we accepted the principle and placed it in the elections act, without taking the steps necessary to make that principle operative.

In other words the Dominion Elections Act says that an Indian may vote if he signs a waiver, but no statute has said what effect the waiver to be signed would have. Therefore this is really only a complementary section to a principle already adopted when we passed the amendments to the Dominion Elections Act.
My second objection is more serious, and perhaps is not a popular one. I would ask the committee to believe that I am just as sincere in my objections as I know the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is in offering his amendment. The effect of the amendment to the Dominion Elections Act in this subsection is not to persuade the Indian to barter away anything; it is to persuade him to accept at one and the same time the rights, privileges, duties and responsibilities of a full-voting Canadian citizen.
I am sure the hon. member who has spoken did not intend to convey the impression, one which I gained from some of his remarks, that the subsection is here to enable the Department of National Revenue to catch up with some Indians. I do not think he meant to convey the impression that our purpose in putting such a section into the laws of this country was in order to collect the few dollars which we might collect.
He has suggested as a basis for his argument that we are taking away from the Indian certain rights which were his of exemption from certain forms of taxation. I suggest that those rights, if that is the proper expression, were given to the Indian as a quid pro quo, as compensation for the fact that we have refused him permission to take full part in the government of this country by expressing his opinion by means of the ballot. I could talk on this for a long time but I am going to conclude with one sentence which I hope will convey my feelings. In this country over a long period of years in recent history we have gradually come to lay more emphasis on rights, ignoring our duties. I suggest that if we are making a real effort to assist the Indian we shall help him to regard duty and rights as going hand in hand.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the discussion has become somewhat general on section 86 I should like to try to lay before the committee what I understand to be the views of the Indians with regard to whether or not in order to receive the vote they should have to give up what had previously been their exemption from taxation. Whether or not we agree with the stand of the Indians it does seem to me that there is a duty on the committee to try to appreciate their point of view.

We must remember that he is an Indian; he is not yet a fully qualified citizen. Therefore I think there is some merit in his contention that he is entitled to an exemption which might confer privileges over and above those enjoyed by white people for the time being. But there is a great deal of substance of right to the Indian's claim. I agree with most of the argument of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, although I am not certain that I agree with his legal argument, that revenues from oil and timber rights would necessarily be capital and therefore not definable as income to be taxed.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: That is correct; that is the best part of the argument.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I am not sure as to the' merits of the hon. member's legal argument. Revenue from oil rights might be derived from lease rentals or simply from the receipts of outright purchase. It seems to me that the part of the hon. member's argument which was most impressive, if he will forgive me for putting it that way, was that part which dealt with the merits of the Indian's claim to be exempt from taxation.
The Indians take the position that they were the original inhabitants of this country, that the white people came and took over the lands and confined the Indians to certain areas and reserves. Those reserves were created by treaty in some cases and in other cases by processes of allotment. Generally speaking, the Indian's argument was that he should be compensated, not only for the loss of the possession of his lands but also for the loss of the general hunting and fishing rights over the lands from which he had derived his living. As compensation we gave him certain privileges which he enjoyed on the reserve. The Indian did not ask to be confined to the reserve; we confined him to the reserve. There is no doubt about that. We must not kid ourselves about this. The Indian did not ask to be put on the reserve; we put him there.
In partial satisfaction of a sense of justice we said to the Indian, "You will enjoy certain privileges on those reserves." The Indian's position throughout the years has been that those privileges which he enjoys in connection with his reserves and in his status as an Indian were conveyed to him in perpetuity in compensation for the losses which he suffered1 at the hands of the white men when they took over the country.
That being the case the Indian says, "Now you come to us and say that you wish to make us citizens by amending the Indian Act; that you wish to bring about a set of circumstances under which the Indian may become enfranchised"-I am using the word 80709-196
Indian Act
"enfranchised" in its proper sense, not merely as conveying the right to vote. "You have told us you want us to be enfranchised, you want us to enjoy equal status with the whites and you want us to accept equal obligations. You say you are doing this for the future of the Indians. You tell us that we should exercise the right and privilege of voting. The first thing you do when you ask us to accept these so-called privileges and to embrace these duties is to give up a privilege which has been ours ever since there were Indians, ever since there were bands and reserves established in the country."
The Indian does not think it is a strong argument when we say that we are trying to encourage him to became a citizen, to enjoy all our benefits and to assume full equality with us when as a first condition we tell him he must give up certain privileges which were given to him in perpetuity. He is unable to appreciate the logic of the argument just put forward by the hon. member for Skeena. I have to confess that were that argument applied to white people its logic would be inescapable, but I do suggest strongly that, when it is applied to Indians who are not yet our equal in status or in many respects our equals in appreciation of logic, it loses much of its force.
We have to deal with this matter to a certain extent from the Indian's point of view. If we want him to be fully equal to the white man, if we want him to assume willingly the duties which go with citizenship and equality, then we might make this one small concession, particularly, as has been pointed * out by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, when there would only be a small proportion of the Indians in receipt of taxable income on the reserves. I think it is proper to compare the situation in Canada with what exists in the United States. I have here a pamphlet issued by Theodore H. Hass, chief counsel of the United States Indian Service, entitled, "Should Indians Vote?" I should like to read one passage, which is as follows:
In. 1924 all Indians bom in the United States, who had not become naturalized by treaty or statute, were made citizens by an act of congress. About 125,000 Indians were affected by this law. As a consequence of attaining national citizenship, Indians automatically became citizens of the state where they reside. Yet on January 26, 1938, seven states still refused to let Indians go to the polls. As a result the solicitor of the department of the interior issued an opinion on the question of whether these state actions were constitutional. The opinion concluded:
"I am of the opinion that the fifteenth amendment clearly prohibits any denial of the right to vote to Indians under circumstances in which non-Indians would be permitted to vote. The laws of Idaho, New Mexico, and Washington which would exclude Indians not taxed from voting in effect exclude citizens of one race from voting on grounds

Indian Act
which are not applied to citizens of other races. For this reason I believe such laws are unconstitutional under the fifteenth amendment. Similarly, the laws of Idaho and South Dakota which would exclude Indians who maintain tribal relations from voting are believed to be unconstitutional as such laws exclude citizens from voting on grounds which apply to only one race."
Section 1 of the fifteenth amendment to the United States constitution, which was adopted on March 30, 1870, provides:
"The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any state or account of race, colour, or previous condition of servitude."
I know, Mr. Chairman, that we are not governed by the United States constitution or the United States bill of rights, but I do suggest that we are here endeavouring to do that thing which the United States apparently has already done, make the Indians full citizens and give them the right to vote. It is argued by the minister, and by such hon. members as the hon. member for Skeena, that the Indian who-and I will put it on their basis-as a previous condition of servitude enjoyed tax exemption cannot be allowed to vote unless he gives up that tax exemption. I would hope that we are not behind the United States in our ideals of citizenship. We have not the fifteenth amendment or anything like it, and it has been argued by ministers of the crown opposite on other occasions that the reason why we do not have these written bills of rights is because they are inherent in our constitution and in our way of life. Yet it seems to me that if we do what is contained in subsection 2 of section 86 we will in effect be denying the right of citizens of Canada to vote on account oi race, colour or previous condition of servitude. That is what we will be doing, the thing which the United States, in accordance with its traditions of freedom and democracy, has made it impossible to do under their fifteenth amendment.
Here in Canada of course I think there is another significant factor, and that is that at least two of the provinces have given the Indian the right to vote in provincial matters. British Columbia, and I believe Saskatchewan, both allow the Indians to vote. Perhaps I should speak only for my own province and say that British Columbia now allows Indians to vote. Whether they live on reserve or off reserve, whether or not they pay income tax, the province does not attach any conditions to the right to vote, and surely this house will not be less generous in its treatment of Indians than one of the provinces of Canada.
In the United States, again according to this pamphlet, apparently the situation was the reverse. The federal government first made them citizens and gave them the right to vote,
IMr. Fulton.]
and certain states denied them that right. The pamphlet dealing with this question contains a passage having to do with a case where one of the states denied Indians the right to vote. It points out that this case was brought before a court, and the court pointed out that the provision designed to prevent people who are unfit or unqualified from voting in an election was not intended to exclude Indians. Then the pamphlet goes on to say:
Three weeks later a three judge federal statutory court granted a permanent Injunction in the case of Trujillo vs. Garley restraining an election clerk from refusing to register a Pueblo Indian and others similarly situated because of a provision of the New Mexico state constitution excluding from the franchise "Indians not taxed."
New Mexico had attempted to restrain Indians from voting unless they gave up their exemption from taxation, and the United States court gave the opinion that this could not be done under the American constitution. Apparently in Canada, in spite of the fine things which are said about this act-and I think the spirit behind the act is a fine spirit -we are going to deny Indians the right to vote unless they give up exemption from taxation. As I pointed out, at least one province of Canada has given them the right to vote with no strings attached. Under the constitution of the United States, having previously enjoyed tax exemption, it has apparently been held that when given the right to vote they shall have that right without the necessity of giving up their tax exemption, and states have been restrained from preventing Indians from voting on the ground that they are tax exempt.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, we can see the force of the Indian argument which I attempted to outline earlier when it is reinforced by the practice and the principle laid down in the United States, which has an Indian problem at least similar to ours. In that country they have accepted the principle that Indians when made citizens shall be given the right to vote without giving up these privileges which we gave in perpetuity in compensation, in the Indians' eyes, for other and vastly greater privileges, the privilege of sole ownership of this country which we took away from them. I would hope that this parliament would be guided by principles and inspired by charity no less than that which appears to guide the citizens of the United States.

reads:
When an order of enfranchisement issues or has been issued, the governor in council may, with the consent of the council of the band, by order declare that any lands within a reserve of which the enfranchised Indian had formerly been in lawful possession shall cease to be Indian reserve lands.
The council of the Six Nations Indians take very strong exception to this section, and always have. They say it will simply dot the Indian, reserve with white owners. Even though the minister has inserted the words "with the consent of the council of the band" they are still fearful that the reserve may become infiltrated with white owners, which in their view would be a very bad; situation. If in connection with land bordering the reserve the council of the band were in agreement I can see no reason why such lands could not be taken out of the reserve; but to pinpoint any reserve with white owners would be very objectionable, and I think would mean the ultimate end of that reserve. Surely the minister could do something in this section to prevent any such thing happening. If the whole band wanted to give up their reserve that would be all right; but to pinpoint it with whites would only mean that the reserve would, be broken up and the only home the Indians feel is theirs would be gradually taken away from them.
